candidates.title: File:Courtyard and Mahabharata Reliefs at the Kailasa Temple, Ellora 01.jpg
candidates.author: Rohit Sharma
candidates.description: The Kailasa Temple at Ellora (Cave 16) is a remarkable example of rock-cut architecture, commissioned in the 8th century by Rashtrakuta king Krishna I. Carved entirely out of a single basalt rock, the temple represents a monolithic excavation rather than constructed assembly, making it one of the largest free-standing rock-cut structures in the world. Architecturally, it is designed as a multi-storeyed complex with a central sanctum (garbhagriha) housing a Shiva lingam, surrounded by intricately sculpted mandapas, pillared halls, and sub-shrines. The temple exhibits precise spatial planning, with axial alignment, carved columns, and elaborately detailed reliefs depicting episodes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, and Puranic traditions. Its technical brilliance lies in the sequential top-down excavation method, extensive use of structural relief, and integration of functional spaces (courtyards, stairways, and water channels) within a single rock mass, exemplifying the apex of early medieval Indian engineering and sculptural artistry.

candidates.title: File:Lascar Ellora caves - Cave 10 (Vishwakarma cave) (4558324543).jpg
candidates.author: Jorge Láscar from Australia
candidates.description: Most famous of the Buddhist caves is cave 10, a chaitya hall (chandrashala) or 'Vishwakarma cave', popularly known as the "Carpenter's Cave". Beyond its multi-storeyed entry is a cathedral-like stupa hall also known as chaitya, whose ceiling has been carved to give the impression of wooden beams. At the heart of this cave is a 15 foot statue of Buddha seated in a preaching pose. Amongst other Buddhsist caves, all of the first nine (caves 1-9) are monasteries. Each of the last two caves, Do Tal (cave 11) and Tin Tal (cave 12) has three stories. [Wikipedia.org]
